idiom_name: JSON.parse plus an allow-list factory registry keyed by a type member
implementation_notes: The json gem can deserialize content-directedly - json_class names the class, json_create builds it, and Marshal reconstructs the whole object graph - but both mechanisms trust the payload, so modern json requires create_additions: true explicitly and RuboCop flags JSON.load and Marshal.load for arbitrary object creation. The safe realization is therefore the manual one: JSON.parse to a Hash, then a frozen registry mapping the tag to a factory lambda (or a class-level type allow-list), with an explicit unknown-type error. Rails' single-table inheritance uses exactly this type-column idea and deserves the same allow-list treatment whenever the column is not fully under the application's control.
code_sketch:
DECODERS = {
  "order.created"   => ->(h) { OrderCreated.new(h.fetch("id"), h.fetch("total")) },
  "order.cancelled" => ->(h) { OrderCancelled.new(h.fetch("id"), h.fetch("reason")) },
}.freeze                                            # allow-list, not constantize

head = JSON.parse(payload)                         # plain Hash: no class metadata
build = DECODERS[head["type"]] or raise UnknownTypeError, head["type"]
build.call(head)
pitfalls: JSON.load and JSON.restore honour json_class and can instantiate arbitrary objects (CVE-2013-0269), so never pass create_additions: true for data you did not produce.
Marshal.load reconstructs any object graph, is unsafe for untrusted input, and couples the cache to the Ruby version - restrict it to trusted, same-version data.

Calling constantize or Object.const_get on a payload-supplied type name is the Rails polymorphism trap: an attacker-chosen class name instantiates unexpected objects, so map tags through a frozen allow-list instead.
